title: Area III review: Airport and Seaplane Base Operations
intro: These questions mix both Tasks of Area III: radio calls, light signals and airport lighting, plus traffic patterns. Most are real arrival and departure situations that use both Tasks at once, just like the checkride.

questions.q: You arrive from the upwind side (the side away from downwind) of a non-towered airport. Field elevation is 820 feet MSL, pattern altitude is 1,000 feet AGL, and no large or turbine airplanes use the field. Using the preferred entry, you cross midfield at 2,320 feet MSL. What comes next?
options: Turn onto downwind right away and descend to 1,820 feet MSL on the downwind leg.
Fly about 2 miles clear, descend to 1,320 feet MSL, then join on a 45° to downwind at midfield.
Fly about 2 miles clear, scan, descend to 1,820 feet MSL, then turn back and join on a 45° to downwind at midfield.
Descend to 1,820 feet MSL while crossing over the runway, then turn downwind on the far side.
questions.why: Cross midfield at least 500 feet above pattern altitude (820 + 1,500 = 2,320 feet MSL). About 2 miles clear, scan, descend to pattern altitude (820 + 1,000 = 1,820 feet MSL), then turn to join on a 45° at midfield [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. Entering while descending creates collision hazards [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].

questions.q: You are a student pilot inbound to Lakeview, a Class D airport, and you have ATIS information Echo. Which call is best, and when?
options: About 15 miles out: "Lakeview Tower, Cessna Four Three Two One X, student pilot, 15 miles south, 3,500, landing with information Echo."
About 15 miles out: "Lakeview Tower, Two One X, 15 south, landing, have numbers."
About 15 miles out: "Lakeview traffic, Cessna 4321X, 15 miles south, any traffic in the area please advise."
About 3 miles out, already inside the Class D: "Lakeview Tower, Cessna Four Three Two One X, landing."
questions.why: Call the tower about 15 miles out [[33:237|AIM 4-3-2a]], and make contact before entering Class D [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(c)]]. Use your full call sign on initial contact [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4a1]], say "student pilot" [[33:231|AIM 4-2-4c]], and name the ATIS code. "Have numbers" does not mean you have the ATIS [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13h]].

questions.q: You plan to land at a non-towered airport with Runways 9-27. On the CTAF, the UNICOM operator says "wind calm, favoring Runway 27." No one else is in the pattern. Overflying well above pattern altitude, you see the wind sock standing out stiff with its large end pointing east. Which runway do you plan to use?
options: Runway 27, because UNICOM gave the official wind.
Runway 27, because it is the calm-wind runway.
Either one, since wind indicators matter only at towered airports.
Runway 9. The wind sock shows a wind from the east, and UNICOM reports have no standards.
questions.why: The large end of a wind sock points into the wind [[33:244|AIM 4-3-4]], so the wind is from the east and Runway 9 is into the wind [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.5]]. Check wind indicators even when the CTAF gives you wind, because that information may not be accurate [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]]. UNICOM has no standards for what it says [[17:5|AC 90-66C 9.3]].

questions.q: In daylight, your radio has died. You have joined the pattern at a Class D airport. On downwind, the tower aims a flashing green light at you. What does it mean, and how do you acknowledge?
options: Cleared to land now. Rock your wings.
Return for landing, and a steady green will follow. Rock your wings.
Airport unsafe, do not land. Rock your wings.
Give way to other aircraft and keep circling. Rock your wings.
questions.why: In flight, a flashing green means return for landing, to be followed by a steady green at the proper time [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. In daylight, acknowledge in flight by rocking your wings [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a2]]. You still need the steady green before you land [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]].

questions.q: Look at the sample airport data. You arrive at night after the part-time tower has closed. The AWOS gives wind 220 at 10, and you will land on Runway 23. How do you fly the pattern and where do you announce?
options: Right traffic for Runway 23, self-announcing on 118.3
Left traffic for Runway 23, self-announcing on 118.3
Right traffic for Runway 23, self-announcing on 122.95
Left traffic for Runway 23, self-announcing on 123.8
questions.why: "RP 23, 34" means Runways 23 and 34 use right traffic [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p. 15]]. With the tower closed, self-announce on the CTAF [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9g2]], and the C after 118.3 shows it is the CTAF [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p. 15]]. 122.95 is the UNICOM and 123.8 is the ATIS.

questions.q: You are on VFR flight following, 18 miles from a non-towered destination, and you no longer need the service. What is the best way to finish up?
options: Squawk 1200 and switch away without a word, since flight following is optional.
Keep the assigned code, switch to the CTAF, and make your first call on downwind.
Tell ATC before leaving the frequency, squawk 1200, then monitor the CTAF and announce about 10 miles out.
Stay with ATC until you enter the pattern, then call on the CTAF from downwind.
questions.why: When you no longer want advisories, tell the controller before changing frequency, then squawk 1200 [[33:215|AIM 4-1-15b2]]. Inbound pilots should monitor and talk on the CTAF from 10 miles to landing [[33:207|AIM 4-1-9c1]].

questions.q: You are on downwind at a non-towered airport, at pattern altitude. A faster Bonanza is catching up from behind at the same altitude. Who has the right-of-way, and what should the Bonanza do?
options: The Bonanza does, because it is faster. You must widen your pattern.
You do. The Bonanza must alter course to the right and pass well clear.
The Bonanza does, because it is behind you. You must climb out of its way.
Neither. Whoever turns base first lands first.
questions.why: The aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way, and the overtaking pilot must alter course to the right to pass well clear [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(f)]]. The right-of-way rules apply all through the pattern [[17:11|AC 90-66C 9.12.4]].

questions.q: On a hazy afternoon, you are 12 miles from a Class D airport and see its rotating beacon on. What should you make of it?
options: It always means IFR, so you can never enter.
It means the tower has closed and the airport is now non-towered.
It means the weather is VFR and the airport is open for pattern work.
It often means the ceiling is below 1,000 feet or visibility below 3 miles, but it is not required. Get the ATIS to know the real weather.
questions.why: In a surface area, a daytime beacon often means visibility below 3 miles and/or a ceiling below 1,000 feet. But there is no requirement for daytime operation, so don't rely on it alone [[33:133|AIM 2-1-9d]]. Listen to the ATIS for the weather before you call the tower [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13c]].

questions.q: You will land on Runway 18 in left traffic. The wind is from 270 (west). On the downwind leg, which way does the wind push you, and how do you correct?
options: Toward the runway. Angle the nose away from the runway.
It doesn't. The wind only matters on final.
Away from the runway. Angle the nose toward the runway, into the wind.
Away from the runway. Fly the runway heading and fix it on base.
questions.why: In left traffic for Runway 18 you fly downwind heading north, east of the runway, so a west wind blows you away from it. Angle into the wind to hold a track parallel to the runway [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. Correcting for drift to keep the proper track is a checkride standard [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

questions.q: You are inbound to a Class D airport. Your receiver seems dead, but your transmitter may work. You stay outside the surface area, figure out the traffic flow, and tell the tower your type, position, altitude, that you will land, and that you need light signals. When do you report your position again?
options: At about 3 to 5 miles out. Then join the pattern and watch the tower for light signals.
Only after you land, since the tower can't answer you anyway.
At 10 miles out, on the CTAF instead of the tower frequency.
Never. With a dead receiver, use only light signals.
questions.why: With a dead receiver: stay outside or above the Class D surface area until you know the flow, then advise the tower. At about 3 to 5 miles, report your position, join the pattern and watch for light signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13a1]]. Squawk 7600 for lost two-way radio [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]].

questions.q: You are on a 1-mile final at a non-towered airport. A pilot behind you calls, "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, Cherokee Five Kilo X-ray, engine failure, landing Runway 22." Who has the right-of-way?
options: You do, because you are on final and lower.
You do, because you are ahead and it may not overtake you.
Whichever airplane is lower, the same as any two landing aircraft.
The Cherokee. An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all others, so give way and keep the frequency quiet.
questions.why: An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other air traffic [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(c)]]. MAYDAY has absolute priority and commands radio silence on the frequency [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1d]].

questions.q: At night over a non-towered airport, you keyed the CTAF 7 times to turn on the runway lights. You then spent 20 minutes checking the wind and setting up. On downwind, the lights go out. What happened, and what do you do?
options: Someone turned them off on purpose. Land on the dark runway.
The lights time out 15 minutes after the last activation. Key the mike 7 times within 5 seconds again.
The lights only stay on for 5 minutes. Key the mike 3 times to restart them.
The system failed. Call UNICOM and ask them to switch the lights on by hand.
questions.why: Pilot-controlled lights stay on for 15 minutes from the most recent activation. Key the mike 7 times first for the highest intensity, then adjust down if you want [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].

questions.q: At night you are cleared straight in to Runway 16 at a towered airport. You are 6 NM out, still about 20° off the extended centerline, and the PAPI already shows two white and two red. Should you start down now?
options: Yes. Two white and two red means you are on glide path, so descend with it.
Yes. PAPI clearance covers you anywhere you can see the lights.
No. The PAPI only gives safe obstacle clearance within 10° of the centerline and out to 3.4 NM. Line up with the runway first.
No. You must wait until the PAPI shows all white.
questions.why: The PAPI typically gives safe obstruction clearance within plus or minus 10° of the extended centerline and out to 3.4 NM. Don't start a descent with it until you are visually aligned with the runway [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]].

questions.q: Tower says, "Cessna Niner Tango Juliet, Runway 31, cleared for takeoff, caution wake turbulence, departing Gulfstream." You decide to go. How do you avoid its wake?
options: Note where the Gulfstream rotated, lift off before that point, and climb above its path.
Lift off after its rotation point, then climb just below its path.
Stay in ground effect well past its rotation point to build speed.
Nothing special. Wake turbulence matters only when landing.
questions.why: Departing behind a larger aircraft: rotate before its rotation point and keep climbing above its climb path until you turn clear of its wake [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Avoid the area below and behind the aircraft making the wake [[17:10|AC 90-66C 9.12.3.1]].

questions.q: At night, 15 miles from your home non-towered airport, the ammeter swings to a full-scale minus reading. What is the best action?
options: The battery is overcharging. Turn off the master switch and continue as planned.
This is normal at night with the lights on. Ignore it.
The battery has several hours left, so continue to your planned stop 90 minutes away.
Your alternator has likely failed. Turn off unneeded electrical equipment and land at the nearest suitable airport.
questions.why: A full-scale minus reading shows an alternator or generator malfunction [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]. Battery time is a rough estimate (about 40 minutes), so reduce the electrical load and land at the nearest suitable airport [[23:330|IFH 11-5]].

questions.q: You fly a low-wing airplane in a busy pattern. Which spot makes it hardest for you and another pilot to see each other?
options: You are just below a high-wing airplane.
You are just above a high-wing airplane.
You are beside a low-wing airplane at the same altitude.
You are beside a high-wing airplane at the same altitude.
questions.why: High wings block the view above, and low wings block the view below. The worst case is a low-wing airplane flying above a high-wing airplane. Bank now and then to clear blind spots [[24:169|AFH 8-5]].

questions.q: On downwind for Runway 27, you hear, "Cessna Four Kilo X-ray, change to Runway 33, make right base, cleared to land." You had pictured Runway 27 the whole flight. Which reply best guards against a mix-up?
options: "Roger."
"Cleared to land, Four Kilo X-ray."
"Runway 33, right base, cleared to land, Cessna Four Kilo X-ray."
Just rock your wings to keep the frequency clear.
questions.why: Read back runway assignments with your call sign, so the numbers get double-checked [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7b]]. Expectation bias can make you hear or fly what you expected [[30:45|RMH 6-2]]. If you are unsure, ask.

questions.q: The tower has issued a wind shear alert. On a 1/2-mile final, your airspeed suddenly drops 15 knots, the airplane sinks, and the PAPI goes from two white and two red to four red. What should you do?
options: Go around right away with full power. This may be a microburst tailwind.
Lower the nose to get the airspeed back and keep landing.
Reduce power to stay on the glide path.
Keep going; the PAPI will bring you back up.
questions.why: A headwind changing to a tailwind cuts airspeed and performance, and on approach a microburst can force you to the ground short of the runway [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Be ready to go around at the first sign; at low altitude recovery may be impossible [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. Four red PAPI lights mean you are low [[33:124|AIM 2-1-2b]].

questions.q: You land at night on a long precision approach runway and float. The runway centerline lights change from alternating red and white to all red. About how much runway is left?
options: About 3,000 feet
About 2,000 feet
About 500 feet
About 1,000 feet
questions.why: Centerline lights are white until the last 3,000 feet, then alternate red and white for the next 2,000 feet, and are all red for the last 1,000 feet [[33:126|AIM 2-1-5a]].

questions.q: At a towered airport, you are on downwind and closing fast on a slower airplane you were told to follow. What is the right fix?
options: Make a 360 to open up space, then tell the tower after.
Slow down or make shallow S-turns, and tell the tower if you need to maneuver.
Pass the slower airplane on its left and land first.
Descend 300 feet and pass underneath it.
questions.why: Adjust power on downwind so you are not too fast or too slow for the traffic [[24:169|AFH 8-5]]. The controller can expect shallow S-turns, but not a 360. Tell the controller if you maneuver for spacing [[33:244|AIM 4-3-5]].

questions.q: On downwind, your aileron control jams. You get it free and land safely. No one is hurt and nothing is damaged. What must you do?
options: Notify the NTSB right away. A flight control malfunction is a serious incident.
Nothing. With no injury or damage, it is not an accident.
File NTSB Form 6120.1/2 within 10 days, but there's no need to call.
Report it only if the FAA asks you to.
questions.why: A flight control system malfunction or failure is a serious incident that requires immediate notice to the NTSB [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5(a)(1)]]. The written report for an incident is needed only if the NTSB asks for it [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]].

questions.q: On short final at a towered airport, the tower says, "Cessna Two Papa Kilo, go around, traffic on the runway." After you add power and start climbing on the upwind leg, where should you fly?
options: Stay right over the runway centerline to keep it under you.
Make a 360 to come back onto final.
Turn gently to one side of the runway so you can keep the runway and any departing traffic in sight.
Level off at 500 feet AGL to stay below departing traffic.
questions.why: After a go-around, once at a safe altitude, make a shallow-bank turn to the side to see the runway and departing aircraft [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. A 360 in the pattern is a major maneuver the controller can't expect [[33:244|AIM 4-3-5]].
